items.s: Each owner holds a specified percentage based on his or her contributions to the account.
items.w: JTIC ownership is divided into percentages tied to each owner’s contributions, unlike the undivided JTWROS interest.

items.s: At one owner’s death, that owner’s share goes to his or her designated beneficiary.
items.w: In a JTIC account the deceased owner’s portion goes to that owner’s beneficiary or estate, not the survivors.

items.s: Two siblings want their shares to pass to their own spouses at death.
items.w: Only JTIC lets each owner leave a separate share to a personally chosen beneficiary such as a spouse.

items.s: The account assets are subject to probate when an owner dies.
items.w: The book states JTIC assets are subject to probate and are distributed as part of the deceased’s estate.

items.s: All owners own 100% of the assets through an undivided interest.
items.w: JTWROS gives each owner an undivided interest in the entire account, so every owner owns 100% of the assets.

items.s: A deceased owner’s interest passes automatically to the surviving owners.
items.w: The right of survivorship means the deceased owner’s interest goes directly to the surviving account owners.

items.s: This title avoids probate and is common for married couples or a parent and adult child.
items.w: JTWROS avoids probate because assets transfer directly to survivors, which is why spouses commonly choose this title.

items.s: A married couple wants the survivor to receive the full account value after one spouse dies.
items.w: Survivorship gives the surviving spouse the entire account, while a JTIC title would split the value.

items.s: The FINRA minimum maintenance requirement is 25% of market value.
items.w: FINRA sets maintenance at 25% of long market value, compared with 30% on short positions.

items.s: Buying $1,500 of stock requires an initial deposit of the full $1,500.
items.w: For a long purchase of $2,000 or less the deposit is 100% of the purchase price.

items.s: The initial minimum is the lesser of $2,000 or 100% of the purchase price.
items.w: The long-side FINRA minimum equity rule is the lesser of $2,000 or the full purchase price.

items.s: A position with $60,000 of market value must keep at least $15,000 of equity.
items.w: Long maintenance is 25% of $60,000, which equals $15,000 of required equity.

items.s: The FINRA maintenance requirement is 30% of market value.
items.w: FINRA sets short maintenance at 30% of short market value, higher than the 25% on long positions.

items.s: Selling $1,500 of stock requires a $2,000 deposit even though that exceeds the sale value.
items.w: Short sales need at least $2,000 even when 100% of the sale price is less than that.

items.s: A position with $60,000 of market value must keep at least $18,000 of equity.
items.w: Short maintenance is 30% of $60,000, which equals $18,000 of required equity.

items.s: The $2,000 minimum applies to sales up to $4,000, with no 100%-of-price alternative.
items.w: Short sales have a flat $2,000 minimum up to $4,000 and never use the lesser-of test.

items.s: Exchange-traded fund shares.
items.w: ETFs are listed on the exchanges and appear on the list of securities the Federal Reserve permits on margin.

items.s: A closed-end fund trading on an exchange.
items.w: Closed-end funds are exchange-traded, so the Federal Reserve Board allows them to be purchased on margin.

items.s: A LEAPS option with 18 months until expiration.
items.w: LEAPS options with more than nine months to expiration are eligible to be purchased on margin.

items.s: Treasury bonds.
items.w: Bonds and fixed-income securities such as Treasury bonds are on the list of margin-eligible securities.

items.s: Mutual fund shares, even though they may later serve as collateral.
items.w: Mutual funds cannot be purchased on margin, though they can be pledged as collateral after 30 days.

items.s: Shares of a new IPO during the first 30 days after the effective date.
items.w: The Federal Reserve Board restricts IPO purchases on margin for the first 30 days after the effective date.

items.s: An option contract with six months until expiration.
items.w: Options with nine months or less until expiration cannot be purchased on margin.

items.s: Annuities.
items.w: Annuities appear on the Federal Reserve’s list of products that may not be purchased on margin.

items.s: The account has exactly one custodian and one minor beneficiary.
items.w: Custodial accounts can have only one custodian and one minor beneficiary, unlike a trust with several beneficiaries.

items.s: The minor’s Social Security number appears on the account, and the minor owes the taxes.
items.w: The minor owns the assets, so the minor’s SSN is used and the minor bears the tax liability.

items.s: Gifts to the account are irrevocable and cannot be taken back by the donor.
items.w: Any gift to a UGMA or UTMA account is irrevocable, so neither donor nor minor can reverse it.

items.s: Margin trading is not permitted in the account.
items.w: The book states margin trading is not permitted in UGMA or UTMA accounts.

items.s: The firm must receive a copy of the agreement, usually written by an attorney, to open the account.
items.w: Trust clients must give the broker-dealer a copy of the trust agreement, which is usually drafted by an attorney.

items.s: The creator may restrict the assets, such as allowing use for educational expenses only.
items.w: A trust lets its creator limit or restrict how the assets are used, which custodial accounts do not.

items.s: It may be revocable, meaning the creator can alter or cancel it.
items.w: Trusts may be revocable or irrevocable, and only a revocable trust can be changed or cancelled by the trustor.

items.s: The controlling person acts under powers and limits written in an agreement and may also be the beneficiary.
items.w: A trustee acts under the trust agreement’s powers, and the trustee and beneficiary may even be the same person.

items.s: The customer must pay in full for securities purchased.
items.w: A cash account requires full payment, so purchases cannot exceed the cash the customer has deposited.

items.s: Failing to pay by the Reg T deadline leads to a sell-out and a 90-day freeze.
items.w: Unpaid cash purchases without an extension are sold out and the account is frozen for 90 days.

items.s: Buying and selling a security without ever paying for it is free-riding here.
items.w: Free-riding is the cash account violation of selling shares that were never paid for.

items.s: The customer may withdraw cash balances at any time, in whole or in part.
items.w: The book says customers have the right to withdraw cash balances held in a cash account at any time.

items.s: The customer signs a hypothecation agreement pledging securities as collateral.
items.w: Hypothecation of account securities as loan collateral is part of the margin agreement, not a cash account requirement.

items.s: Every short sale must be executed here.
items.w: All short sales must be placed in a margin account because the shares are borrowed.

items.s: The account is marked to the market daily, and falling equity triggers maintenance calls.
items.w: Margin accounts, long and short, are marked to market daily to test the maintenance requirement.

items.s: A margin disclosure statement must be delivered at opening and annually.
items.w: FINRA Rule 2264 requires the margin disclosure statement before or at opening and every year.

items.s: Must be delivered to the customer at or before settlement of the trade.
items.w: Confirmations are due at or before completion of the transaction, which the rule defines as settlement.

items.s: Shows the mark-up or mark-down when the firm acted as principal.
items.w: Principal trades require the confirmation to show the mark-up or mark-down; agency trades show commission.

items.s: Identifies the security traded by its CUSIP number.
items.w: The CUSIP ID uniquely identifying the security is a required confirmation item for the trade.

items.s: A municipal bond version must show yield to worst and accrued interest.
items.w: MSRB Rule G-15 adds yield to worst, accrued interest, and call features to municipal trade confirmations.

items.s: Sent at least quarterly to customers with positions, a money balance, or activity.
items.w: FINRA Rule 2231 requires quarterly statements for any account with securities, a money balance, or activity.

items.s: Must be sent monthly when the account holds options or penny stocks.
items.w: Holding options or penny stocks raises the required statement frequency from quarterly to monthly.

items.s: Provides a snapshot of the account as of the closing date.
items.w: The statement is a snapshot of the account’s status on its closing date, letting customers spot errors.

items.s: Not required for an inactive account holding no securities and no money balance.
items.w: Statements go only to customers with a position, balance, or activity since the last statement.

items.s: Protects up to $500,000 per separate customer, with no more than $250,000 in cash.
items.w: SIPC limits are $500,000 per separate customer including at most $250,000 in cash.

items.s: A nonprofit membership corporation that is not an agency of the US government.
items.w: SIPC is a not-for-profit corporation created by Congress and funded by broker-dealer assessments.

items.s: Coverage depends on the account title, so one person can be several separate customers.
items.w: Individual, joint, trust, IRA, Roth IRA, and minor accounts each count as separate customers for SIPC.

items.s: A customer whose claim exceeds the limit becomes a general creditor of the failed firm.
items.w: Once SIPC limits are exceeded, the customer holds only a general creditor claim against the broker-dealer.

items.s: Insures checking, savings, and bank-issued CDs at banks and thrifts.
items.w: FDIC coverage is limited to bank deposit products such as checking, savings, money market accounts, and CDs.

items.s: Coverage is $250,000 per depositor in each bank, backed by US government full faith and credit.
items.w: FDIC insurance of at least $250,000 per depositor is backed by the full faith and credit of the government.

items.s: Does not cover mutual funds or stocks, even when they are purchased through a bank.
items.w: Securities and mutual funds are not FDIC insured, even if sold by a bank branch.

items.s: An independent agency created by Congress in 1933 that also supervises failed banks.
items.w: The FDIC was created in 1933 and also examines institutions and manages receiverships of failed banks.
